V01-I-001: In many countries a tip began as an optional gift, a small reward a diner left for service that seemed unusually attentive. Over time, however, the gift hardened into an expectation, and leaving nothing came to be read as a complaint rather than as ordinary behaviour. Once that happened, employers in some trades began to treat tips as part of the wage and set basic pay lower in anticipation of them. The result is a curious reversal: with basic pay cut to match, a custom meant to reward exceptional service now props up the ordinary income of the people who provide it.
V01-I-002: Most trees in temperate climates add one ring of wood each year, wide in good growing seasons and narrow in poor ones. Because the weather of a region varies from year to year, trees growing there share a recognisable sequence of wide and narrow rings. By matching this sequence in living trees with the inner rings of old beams and buried logs, researchers can extend the pattern far into the past. A wooden object of unknown date can then be placed in time by finding where its own rings fit within that long master sequence.
V01-I-003: When electricity first reached homes, there was no agreed way of connecting an appliance to the supply, and manufacturers designed their own plugs. As national grids grew, each country eventually settled on a standard of its own, chosen to suit its voltage and its existing wiring. These national choices, sensible at the time, have left the world with many incompatible socket designs. Travellers who now carry a bag of adapters to cope with them are paying, in a small way, for decisions that were made separately long ago.
V01-I-004: Radio was once a medium of the living room, heard by a whole family gathered around a single set. The podcast, by contrast, is usually heard alone, through earphones, while its listener walks, cooks or commutes. This private setting changes how presenters speak: they drop the formal address of the broadcaster and talk as if to one friend. Listeners, in turn, often feel that they know a presenter personally, though the presenter has never heard of them.
V01-I-005: Homework for young children is often defended on the ground that it builds habits of independent study. Yet a seven-year-old rarely works independently at home; a parent usually sits beside the child, explaining and correcting. What the homework measures, then, is partly the time and education of the parent rather than the effort of the pupil. For this reason some schools have replaced written tasks for the youngest classes with reading aloud, which any family can support.
V01-I-006: Early television comedies were often recorded in front of a studio audience, whose laughter was captured along with the dialogue. When producers began filming without an audience, they found that jokes seemed flat to viewers at home without that sound. Their solution was the laugh track, recorded laughter added afterwards to tell viewers where the funny moments were. Critics soon complained that the device was manipulative, since it instructed the audience to laugh instead of letting them decide. Partly in answer to such complaints, many recent comedies have abandoned it altogether, trusting viewers to find the jokes for themselves.
V01-I-007: Snow falling on the polar ice sheets traps small bubbles of air as it is compressed, year after year, into solid ice. Each bubble is therefore a tiny sample of the atmosphere as it was when that layer of snow was buried. By drilling deep cores and analysing the air in successive layers, scientists can read off how the composition of the atmosphere has changed. The deepest of these cores carry the record back many hundreds of thousands of years, far beyond any written history.
V01-I-008: Insurance exists to spread the cost of misfortunes that no single person could easily bear. But by softening the cost of a loss, it can also weaken the care people take to avoid one. A driver whose car is fully covered, for instance, may park in a street he would otherwise avoid. Insurers respond by making the insured bear a part of every claim, so that carelessness still costs something.
V01-I-009: A translator of prose can usually carry a sentence's meaning into another language and let its rhythm fall where it may. Poetry allows no such freedom, because in a poem the sound and the sense are bound together. A line that keeps the meaning of the original but loses its music has kept only half of what the poet made. Yet the opposite course is no safer, for a translator who chases the rhyme and metre must often bend the meaning to fit them. Every translation of a poem is thus a choice about which loss to accept, and no choice avoids loss entirely.
V01-I-010: Finding one's way through an unfamiliar city once required building a mental map, noting landmarks and the turns between them. Satellite navigation removes that burden, issuing each turn at the moment it is needed. Convenient as this is, it means the traveller can reach a destination without ever forming a picture of the route. Some researchers worry that skills of spatial memory, like other unused abilities, may weaken when they are no longer exercised.
V01-I-011: Many hearing people assume that a sign language is simply a spoken language spelled out on the hands. In fact, the sign languages of deaf communities have their own grammars, often quite unlike that of the spoken language around them. A sign language may, for example, mark a question with the eyebrows and place characters at points in space to track who did what to whom. Such features show that these are full languages in their own right, not manual codes for some other tongue.
V01-I-012: During adolescence the body's internal clock shifts later, so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy and wake later than younger children. School timetables, however, are usually set for the convenience of transport and of working parents, and often begin early in the morning. The two schedules collide, leaving many teenagers chronically short of sleep on school days. Some districts that have moved the start of the day later report pupils who are more alert in morning classes, though the effect on results is still debated.
V01-I-013: Suppose several firms bid for the right to drill in an oilfield whose true value no one knows. Each firm makes its own estimate, and while some estimates will be too high and others too low, their average may be close to the truth. The firm that wins, however, is the one that bid most, which usually means the one whose estimate was most optimistic. Winning is therefore itself a sign that the winner has probably overpaid. Experienced bidders learn to shade their offers below their estimates, precisely to protect themselves from this effect.
V01-I-014: Animals that evolve on remote islands often meet no large predators for thousands of generations. Over that time, defences that cost energy, such as flight or a fear of strangers, tend to fade. When ships bring rats, cats or snakes to such an island, the native birds face hunters they have no means of escaping. This is why island species make up a disproportionate share of recorded extinctions, though islands cover a small part of the earth's land.
V01-I-015: To a concert audience the conductor can seem the least necessary person on stage, the only one who makes no sound. Yet a large orchestra cannot keep together by listening alone, since players at opposite ends of the stage hear one another a fraction of a second late. The conductor's beat gives them a shared visual signal that reaches everyone at the same instant. Much of the real work, moreover, is done before the concert, in rehearsals where the conductor decides how the piece should sound.
V01-I-016: Autocorrect was designed to catch the slips of fingers on small keyboards, replacing an unknown string of letters with the nearest familiar word. Its weakness follows from the same design: when a writer intends an unusual name or a technical term, the software confidently substitutes something common. Because the substitute is a real word, it passes the quick glance that would have caught an ordinary typing error. Autocorrect thus trades a large number of obvious mistakes for a smaller number of subtle ones, which may be the harder kind to notice.
V01-I-017: For years newspapers gave their articles away online, hoping that advertising would pay for the journalism. Advertising revenue, however, flowed increasingly to the large platforms that controlled where readers found the news. Many papers responded by putting their reporting behind a paywall and asking readers to subscribe. This has steadied the finances of some titles, but it has also divided readers into those who pay for careful reporting and those who rely on whatever is free. The worry is that the second group, often the larger, is left with the material least worth trusting.
V01-I-018: In a multiple-choice test, a candidate who knows nothing can still score by guessing. Negative marking is meant to remove this advantage by deducting marks for each wrong answer. Set at the right level, the penalty makes blind guessing worthless on average, while still rewarding a candidate who can eliminate some options. That reward reaches only those willing to claim it, however: some cautious candidates leave blank even questions they could narrow down, so the scheme measures nerve as well as knowledge.
V01-I-019: A gift card looks like a sensible compromise between a present and cash: it lets the recipient choose, while still showing that the giver thought of a particular shop. For the retailer, however, its chief attraction lies less in the sale it records than in the spending it never has to honour. A noticeable share of cards is lost, forgotten or left with a balance too small to bother with, and the value they carry then stays with the seller. One might expect such losses to make people wary of the cards, but the loss is spread thinly and felt by no one in particular, since the giver never sees it and the recipient rarely notices it. Retailers can therefore promote the cards energetically without provoking the resentment that a visible charge of the same size would arouse.
V01-I-020: That migrating birds find their way across continents has never been in doubt; what has resisted explanation is the means. Experiments that altered the magnetic field around caged birds changed the direction in which they tried to fly, which pointed to a magnetic sense. The trouble was that no one could find the organ responsible, and a sense without an organ struck many biologists as no sense at all. That objection assumed that a sense must be housed in some visible structure, whereas this one might operate through molecules in the eye or particles scattered in tissue.
V01-I-021: It is tempting to think that a strict form, with its fixed count of lines and its demanding rhyme scheme, can only hamper a poet. Yet the constraint can work the other way, since the need to find a rhyme pushes the poet past the first, obvious phrase towards one that would otherwise never have been reached. The form, on this view, is less a cage than an instrument of search, a way of making the mind try possibilities it would have skipped. If that is right, free verse, which offers no such instrument, may be harder to write well than it looks.
V01-I-022: A great deal of the code that businesses rely on every day is maintained, without pay, by a handful of volunteers. In the early life of a project this arrangement works well enough, since the people who write the code are also the people who use it. As the project grows popular, its users multiply far faster than its maintainers, and most of them contribute nothing but requests. The few volunteers end up answering complaints instead of writing code, and some of them simply walk away. When they do, companies that had treated the software as free discover that it was free only because someone else was paying with time.
V01-I-023: Grouping pupils by ability appears to help everyone, since teachers can pitch each lesson to the level of the class in front of them. The appearance depends on treating a pupil's placement as a measurement of what that pupil can do. In practice the placement also shapes what the pupil will be able to do, because lower groups are usually taught less and expected to achieve less. A judgement made at eleven can thus become self-confirming, as the groups grow further apart each year and seem to prove the original sorting right.
V01-I-024: A franchise lets an entrepreneur buy into a proven formula rather than invent one, paying fees in return for the brand, the methods and the suppliers. The fees, though, are not the real price; what the franchisee surrenders in exchange for less uncertainty is the freedom to decide. The owner of a franchised cafe, for instance, may not change the menu, the decor or the opening hours, even where local customers would plainly prefer something else. Whether the bargain is a good one depends on which a particular entrepreneur values more: freedom to experiment or protection from the cost of experiments that fail.
V01-I-025: A novelist who wants readers to hear the speech of a region must decide how far to let spelling follow sound. Respelling words as they are pronounced looks like the most faithful course, and many earlier novelists took it freely. Its cost is that the reader meets the speech as a page of misspellings, and misspelling, on the page, suggests ignorance rather than an accent. Worse, characters rendered this way can come to seem less intelligent than the narrator who describes them in standard spelling, an effect the novelist seldom intends. Many later writers have therefore kept conventional spelling for dialogue and conveyed the region through vocabulary, idiom and the rhythm of the sentence.
